title: Approved because State law says so
question: How much housing now goes through under State laws that require approval without a hearing when a project meets written standards?
finding: The Planning Department’s records mark 183 housing project applications since 2017 under a State streamlining law or describe them as ministerial: 11,117 homes proposed, 7,733 of them in the 91 applications approved so far, 6,339 of them below market rate. The count rose from 8 applications opened in 2019 to 52 in 2025. The laws named most: SB 35 (76); SB 9 (55); SB 423 (22); described as ministerial (22); AB 2011 (12). Building permits linked to these applications declare $2.79 billion of construction. The City’s own reports to the State list 74 projects (5,907 homes) as approved under a streamlining law from 2018 to 2025.
how: Project records in the Planning Department’s table that carry the department’s own flag for SB 35, AB 2162 or a Housing Sustainability District, or whose description names SB 35, SB 423, SB 9, AB 2011, AB 2162 or SB 684 or uses the word “ministerial”, grouped by the year the record was opened. Homes are the proposed units on the record; value is the declared cost of the building permits the record lists. The State figure counts San Francisco rows of the housing department’s annual progress report whose streamlining column is not blank or “N”, one per project. SB and AB stand for State Senate and Assembly bills.
limits: Automatic approval of housing that meets the code is State policy, and this is that policy at work; 57% of the homes proposed this way are below market rate. Each record is still assigned to a planner and closes with an approval letter, and a building permit follows as for any project. Records are found by flags and by words in a description, so a project is missed if neither is present and counted twice if it was re-filed; accessory dwelling units are not counted because the records do not mark which were approved this way. A proposed home is not a built home. No applicant or address is listed. What would settle the totals: the Planning Department’s own list of ministerial approvals.
